questions.title: Why does BLT use a separate entropy model for patching instead of the global transformer's own predictions?
questions.question_body: In the BLT paper, Section 2.3 describes using a separate small byte-level LM (100M parameters) to compute next-byte entropies for determining patch boundaries. This seems redundant — why not use the global latent transformer's own uncertainty estimates to decide where patch boundaries should be? Wouldn't the global model's predictions be more accurate since it has more capacity? Is the entropy model used purely for efficiency, or is there a deeper architectural reason for keeping patching decoupled from the main model?

questions.title: How does increasing the entropy threshold affect average patch size?
questions.question_body: In Section 2.3 of the BLT paper, entropy patching identifies patch boundaries when the next-byte entropy $H(x_t)$ exceeds a threshold $\theta_g$ (global constraint) or when the entropy increase exceeds $\theta_r$ (approximate monotonic constraint). I'm confused about the relationship between the threshold value and the resulting patch size. If I raise $\theta_g$, does that mean fewer bytes qualify as boundaries, leading to longer patches on average? The paper mentions adjusting the threshold from 0.6 to 0.1 at inference time for task performance — does lowering the threshold create more (shorter) patches, and if so, why would that improve task performance?

questions.title: How can BLT simultaneously increase model size and patch size while keeping inference FLOPs fixed?
questions.question_body: Section 5.3 of the BLT paper claims that BLT 'can simultaneously increase model size and patch size while maintaining the same inference flop budget.' I understand that larger patches mean the global latent transformer runs on fewer steps, which saves FLOPs. But if you increase the model size (more parameters in the global transformer), wouldn't each step become more expensive? How do these two effects cancel out exactly? The paper says longer patch sizes save compute 'which can be reallocated to grow the size of the global latent transformer, because it is run less often' — but this seems hand-wavy. Is there a precise mathematical relationship between patch size and model size that preserves FLOPs?

questions.title: What does the parameter $k$ represent in BLT's FLOP estimation, and why is $V=0$ for some components?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.6, the FLOP estimation formula for BLT includes a parameter $k$ described as 'the ratio of patch-dimension to byte-dimension i.e. the number of local model splits that concatenate to form a global model representation ($k=2$ in Figure 3).' I don't understand what 'local model splits' means here. Also, the formula sets $V=0$ for the global transformer and encoder but $V=256$ for the decoder. I assume $V$ is the vocabulary size for the output projection — does this mean only the decoder produces byte predictions, and the global transformer has no output projection at all? How does the global transformer's output get used if it doesn't project to a vocabulary?

questions.title: Why is BPE not an incremental patching scheme, and why does this matter for generation?
questions.question_body: Section 2.4 of the BLT paper defines the incremental patching property as $f_p(\pmb{x}_{<i}) = f_p(\pmb{x})_{<i}$, and states that BPE fails this because 'the same prefix can be tokenized differently depending on the continuation sequence.' I understand the formal definition, but I'm struggling with the practical implication. During autoregressive generation with BPE, the model generates one token at a time — so doesn't it already commit to a tokenization as it goes? Why would future tokens retroactively change how earlier bytes are tokenized? Could someone provide a concrete example where BPE gives different tokens for the same prefix depending on what comes after?

questions.title: How do hash n-gram embeddings avoid the collision problem?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.1.1, BLT introduces hash n-gram embeddings that map byte n-grams through a hash function (RollPolyHash modulo the embedding table size) to an embedding table $E_n^{hash}$. With 500,000 hash entries and n-gram sizes from 3 to 8, there must be massive collisions — many different n-grams will hash to the same embedding. How does this not degrade performance? The paper claims these embeddings are 'vital to bringing the performance of BLT to match those of tokenizer based models,' but I don't understand how a lossy hashing scheme can be so important. Is the idea that collisions don't matter because the model learns to handle them, or that the statistical distribution of hash collisions is somehow benign?

questions.title: How does the encoder cross-attention handle patches of variable byte length?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.1.2, the encoder cross-attention module initializes patch queries by pooling byte representations corresponding to each patch $p_j$, and each query $Q_j$ 'only attends to the keys and values that correspond to the bytes in patch $j$.' Since patches have dynamically determined, variable lengths, different patches will have different numbers of bytes. How does the cross-attention mechanism handle this variability? Is the attention computed per-patch with different-sized key/value sets? And how does max-pooling (mentioned in Section 4.7) work when some patches have 2 bytes and others have 20?

questions.title: Why does the local decoder need encoder hidden states as input?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.2, the local decoder takes as input 'the hidden representations produced by the local encoder for the byte-sequence' (specifically $h_{l_{\mathcal{E}}}$, the output of the last encoder layer). This seems odd — why would the decoder need information from the encoder? The decoder's job is to take global patch representations $o_j$ and produce bytes $y_i$. If the decoder already has the patch representations from the global transformer, what additional information does it get from the encoder's hidden states? Is this related to autoregressive decoding where the decoder needs byte-level context from previously generated bytes?

questions.title: Why do larger patch sizes perform better at larger model scales?
questions.question_body: In Section 5.1, the paper observes that 'BLT with patch size of 8 starts at a significantly worse point compared to BPE Llama 2 at 1B but ends up better than BPE at 7B scale,' and suggests larger patch sizes perform better at larger scales. The paper attributes this 'in part, to the decreasing share of total FLOPs used by the byte-level Encoder and Decoder modules.' But I don't follow this logic. If the local models become a smaller fraction of total compute, how does that explain why larger patches (which reduce global transformer FLOPs) become more favorable? Is the argument that at larger scales, the global transformer is so dominant that you can afford to reduce its frequency without much quality loss?

questions.title: How can initializing BLT's global transformer from Llama 3 work if the input representations are fundamentally different?
questions.question_body: Section 6.2 describes initializing BLT's global transformer with Llama 3.1's weights and training with a lower learning rate. But Llama 3 processes token embeddings from a 128K vocabulary, while BLT's global transformer processes patch representations produced by the local encoder from raw bytes. These are fundamentally different input distributions. How can the same weights work for both? Is the assumption that the latent representation space is similar enough that the transformer's intermediate layers transfer? What about the input embedding layer — does BLT's global transformer even have one, since patches are produced by cross-attention rather than looked up from an embedding table?

questions.title: What is 'entropy drift' and why does resetting context help?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.4, the paper discusses using 'approximate monotonicity constraint' for the large-scale BLT-Entropy run because it 'suffers less from entropy drift from changes in context length.' They also reset the entropy model's context with new lines. I don't understand what 'entropy drift' means here. Is the entropy model's predicted entropy systematically biased by the length of its context window? Why would structured content like multiple choice tasks (mentioned in the MMLU example) cause progressively larger patches? And how does resetting the context with new lines fix this?

questions.title: How does the block-causal attention mask work with dynamic patch boundaries?
questions.question_body: The BLT paper mentions that the global latent transformer uses a 'block-causal attention mask' where 'attention is restricted to be up to and including the current patch within the current document.' But since patch boundaries are dynamically determined and patches have variable sizes, how is this mask constructed efficiently? In standard transformers, causal masks have a simple triangular structure. Does BLT need to construct a custom mask for every sequence based on its patch boundaries? The paper mentions using FlexAttention for this — is this a significant computational overhead compared to standard attention?
